original_question: Let {e} = G_0 subset G_1 subset G_2 subset ... be a tower of groups, let P(G) be its splitting diagram, and fix r > 0. Show that if the tower is r-differential then P(G) is isomorphic to Y^{⊗ r} and there exists an Abelian group A of order r, independent of n, such that G_n is isomorphic to A wreath S_n for all n >= 0; and show that if the tower is r-dual then P(G) is isomorphic to a product (d_1 Y) x ... x (d_k Y) and there exists a group H of order r, independent of n, such that G_n is isomorphic to H wreath S_n for all n >= 0.
target_in_paper: Problem 46 in Section 2 ("Problems of 2025") of arXiv:2509.25446; that problem explicitly points to Christian Gaetz's classification conjecture for r-dual and r-differential towers of groups, cited there as [Gaetz2018, Conj. 1.6] and appearing in the published version as Conjecture 7. ([theworld.com](https://theworld.com/~worley/Math/problem-notebook.pdf))
correct_elements: Your draft captures the correct two-part classification target: in the multiplicity-free r-differential case, the tower should come from a fixed abelian wreath-product tower with Young-lattice branching; in the general r-dual case, the tower should come from a fixed wreath-product tower by a group of order r, with branching graph a product of weighted copies of Young's lattice. It also correctly keeps the group of order r independent of n. ([theworld.com](https://theworld.com/~worley/Math/problem-notebook.pdf))
missing_details: The source treats this as an open conjectural classification problem, not as a theorem already proved in full generality; only the cases r = 1 and r prime are proved in the cited source. ([combinatorics.org](https://www.combinatorics.org/ojs/index.php/eljc/article/download/v26i1p25/pdf/))

The tower must consist of finite groups, and the representation-theoretic operators are defined on the direct sum R(G) = ⊕_{n≥0} R(G_n) of complex representation rings. ([combinatorics.org](https://www.combinatorics.org/ojs/index.php/eljc/article/download/v26i1p25/pdf/))

P(G) should be defined precisely as the Bratteli (splitting) diagram of the tower: vertices are irreducible complex representations of the G_n, and edge multiplicities are the branching multiplicities under restriction/induction. ([theworld.com](https://theworld.com/~worley/Math/problem-notebook.pdf))

The exact meaning of r-dual is the operator identity Res Ind - Ind Res = rI on R(G), equivalently that P(G) is an r-dual graded graph. ([combinatorics.org](https://www.combinatorics.org/ojs/index.php/eljc/article/download/v26i1p25/pdf/))

The exact meaning of r-differential is: G is r-dual and every branching rule G_i ⊂ G_{i+1} is multiplicity-free; equivalently the edge multiplicities in P(G) are all 0 or 1, so P(G) is an r-differential poset. ([theworld.com](https://theworld.com/~worley/Math/problem-notebook.pdf))

Y should be identified explicitly as Young's lattice, and the source uses the r-fold Cartesian product Y^r rather than tensor-product notation Y^{⊗ r}. ([combinatorics.org](https://www.combinatorics.org/ojs/index.php/eljc/article/download/v26i1p25/pdf/))

In part (b), dY must be defined: it is the d^2-dual graded graph whose underlying simple graph is Y and whose edge multiplicities are all multiplied by d. ([combinatorics.org](https://www.combinatorics.org/ojs/index.php/eljc/article/download/v26i1p25/pdf/))

The quantifier on n should be normalized: the notebook writes n ≥ 0, while the cited source states n > 0 and separately adopts the convention A wr S_0 = {e} and A wr S_1 = A. ([theworld.com](https://theworld.com/~worley/Math/problem-notebook.pdf))

The phrase 'independent of n' should be made explicit as: there exists one fixed group A (respectively H) of order r that works for every rank n in the tower. ([theworld.com](https://theworld.com/~worley/Math/problem-notebook.pdf))

The asserted isomorphisms P(G) ≅ Y^r and P(G) ≅ (d_1Y) × ··· × (d_kY) are isomorphisms of graded graphs with multiplicities, not merely of abstract unweighted graphs. ([combinatorics.org](https://www.combinatorics.org/ojs/index.php/eljc/article/download/v26i1p25/pdf/))
refined_question: Open problem. Let G : {e} = G_0 ⊂ G_1 ⊂ G_2 ⊂ ··· be a tower of finite groups. Let R(G) = ⊕_{n≥0} R(G_n), where R(G_n) is the complex representation ring of G_n, and let Ind, Res : R(G) → R(G) be the operators induced by induction and restriction along G_n ⊂ G_{n+1}. Let P(G) be the Bratteli (splitting) diagram of the tower: its vertices are the irreducible complex representations of the groups G_n, and the multiplicity of an edge records the corresponding branching multiplicity. Fix r ∈ Z_{>0}. Assume G is an r-dual tower of groups, meaning that Res Ind - Ind Res = rI on R(G); if, in addition, every branching multiplicity is 0 or 1, call G an r-differential tower of groups. Is it true that: (a) if G is r-differential, then P(G) is isomorphic, as a graded graph, to the r-fold Cartesian product Y^r of Young's lattice, and there exists a fixed abelian group A of order r such that G_n ≅ A wr S_n for every n > 0; and (b) if G is r-dual, then P(G) is isomorphic to (d_1Y) × ··· × (d_kY), where dY denotes the graded graph with underlying simple graph Y and all edge multiplicities multiplied by d, and there exists a fixed finite group H of order r such that G_n ≅ H wr S_n for every n > 0? ([combinatorics.org](https://www.combinatorics.org/ojs/index.php/eljc/article/download/v26i1p25/pdf/))
justification: The draft is unmistakably targeting Problem 46 of the notebook: its two-part structure, the phrases 'not depending on n', the Young-lattice factors, and the wreath-product conclusions match that problem almost verbatim. But Problem 46 is only a brief problem-book restatement; to make it fully stand-alone and faithful, one has to import the actual definitions from Gaetz's paper, namely Definition 4 (r-dual tower via Res Ind - Ind Res = rI), the multiplicity-free characterization of r-differential towers, and Example 5's interpretation of the model towers A wr S and H wr S and of the notation dY. The other major correction is logical status: the paper presents the statement as a conjecture/open problem in general, with only the cases r = 1 or r prime proved by Theorem 6. ([theworld.com](https://theworld.com/~worley/Math/problem-notebook.pdf))
